title: Draupadi spares her sons' killer
hookLine: her sons' killer is dragged before her in ropes, and in the Bhagavata she asks for his life: kshama, mercy that doesn't erase the harm
carry: kshama, forbearance, is a mark of dharma
last: A LEAF OFFERED WITH LOVE IS ENOUGH FOR GOD.

cards: Ropes around his arms, Ashvatthama is pushed forward and made to stand in front of her. He is the son of Drona, the Pandavas' own teacher.
On the last night of the war he crept into their sleeping camp and killed Draupadi's sons. Arjuna has caught him and tied him up like an animal. Krishna has told Arjuna he may kill him.

Instead, Arjuna brings him to the mother of the dead. Last year on this path, the Mahabharata's telling of this moment ended with a jewel. Today the Bhagavata Purana tells it, and she says something else.

teach.h: SHE BOWS TO THE BOUND MAN
teach.b: In the Bhagavata Purana's first book, Draupadi sees the son of her husbands' teacher bound and ashamed, and she bows to him. Then she speaks, in paraphrase. Let him go.
He is the son of the teacher from whom you learned your bows and weapons; in him, the teacher is still here.

teach.h: LET HIS MOTHER NOT WEEP AS I DO
teach.b: Then the line the scene turns on: his mother, Kripi, is still alive. Don't let her weep the way I am weeping now.
The text calls her words fair, kind and full of dharma. Bhima does not agree: this man killed sleeping children, he says, and deserves to die. Krishna finds a way through.
Arjuna cuts the jewel from Ashvatthama's head and shaves his hair, a punishment the text treats as a kind of death for one like him, and sends him out alive.
In the Mahabharata's own telling, Draupadi asks for the jewel; in the Bhagavata, she asks for his life. Readers have held both. Here's the teaching.

Hinduism has a word for what she does: kshama, forbearance, the strength not to strike back when you could. The law book of Manu lists it among the ten marks of dharma, beside truth and freedom from anger.
And notice what kshama isn't. Her grief doesn't vanish; she names it.

teach.h: MERCY, AND THE PUNISHMENT STILL FALLS
teach.b: The punishment still falls. She doesn't ask what he deserves. She asks who else will be sitting where she is sitting tonight.

how: Hindus who read or hear the Bhagavata Purana meet this scene early in its first book, sometimes in long public recitations, and storytellers set it beside the Mahabharata's own telling.

o: a queen who keeps her grief hidden from the whole court
the grieving mother who asks for her sons' killer's life
a mother who forgives and lets the harm go unpunished

games.q: the man in ropes — tap the pairs.
p: son of Drona, the Pandavas' teacher

s: in the Bhagavata, Draupadi demands Ashvatthama's death
in the Bhagavata she asks for his life; in the Mahabharata she asks for the jewel from his head.
Draupadi's reason is that his mother should not weep as she does
she names Kripi, and her own weeping.
Ashvatthama walks free with no punishment at all
his jewel is cut away and his hair shaved, and he is sent out of the camp.

games.q: in Hindu teaching, is kshama, forbearance, the same as pretending a harm never happened?
o: no. Draupadi asked mercy, and the punishment still fell.
yes. real mercy cancels every consequence.
no. kshama means waiting quietly for revenge.
games.why: Draupadi named her grief and asked for his life; Arjuna still took the jewel and sent him out. Manu counts kshama among the ten marks of dharma, beside truth and freedom from anger.

practice: Bring to mind someone who hurt you, small or large; you don't have to forgive them in this sit, and kshama never means the harm didn't happen.
Just look past the person, once, to someone who loves them, a mother, a child, a friend, and let that person be there for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold that other person in prayer.
If the hurt is still happening, or grief is too much, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi. In the Bhagavata, with her sons' killer in ropes before her, she asks for his life so that his mother won't weep as she does. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Draupadi, Drupada's daughter, the woman who asks for mercy in the Bhagavata's telling.

carryVoice: Your line: kshama, forbearance, is a mark of dharma. Draupadi saw another mother. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.7 (Ashvatthama brought bound before Draupadi; her plea for his release; Kripi; the jewel and the shaving)
Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva (Draupadi's fast and the jewel; Critical Edition 10.11–16)
Manusmriti 6.92 (the ten marks of dharma, including kshama, forbearance, and akrodha, freedom from anger)
